paper.title: Best-of- N N Guidance for Test-time Diffusion Alignment
paper.abstract: Abstract Diffusion models achieve strong generative performance but often struggle to align generated samples with human preferences measured by a reward model. A simple yet effective algorithm for test-time alignment is Best-of- N N (BoN) sampling, which draws N N i.i.d. samples from a pre-trained diffusion model and outputs the single highest-reward sample. Despite its empirical success, BoN makes limited use of reward information, as it is incorporated only at the final selection stage without influencing the reverse diffusion trajectory during sampling. Consequently, BoN sampling does not improve the average alignment of generated samples and is primarily suited to single-output settings. We propose Best-of- N N Guidance (BoNG), a novel method that integrates the principle of BoN sampling directly into the reverse diffusion process. BoNG performs online BoN selection over denoising particles and adjusts the reverse diffusion process to steer the particle population toward higher-reward regions during generation. Specifically, by introducing an asymmetric guidance interaction among denoising particles, BoNG uses the current BoN particle as a guidance signal to the rest of the particle population. This particle-level interaction reshapes the sampling process toward higher-reward regions, enabling BoNG to improve not only the final best sample beyond Vanilla BoN sampling, but also the average quality of generated samples. Over 36 empirical comparisons, BoNG achieves the best performance in 29 cases, ranking first in 80.56% of the comparisons against SMC and Vanilla BoN sampling. BoNG also supports multi-output capability, achieving 1.3 × \times ImageReward score of the latest sample-based guidance method with a 1.6 × \times speedup. We release the code at https://github.com/aailab-kaist/BoNG .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion models Sohl-Dickstein et al. (2015) ; Ho et al. (2020) ; Song et al. (2021) demonstrate strong generative capabilities, leading to a growing number of real-world applications that produce outputs conditioned on user inputs Microsoft Team (2026) ; xAI Team (2026) . However, the generated outputs still do not fully align with user preferences in terms of input alignment and sample fidelity. To address this issue, reward functions Xu et al. (2023) ; Wu et al. (2023) ; Ma et al. (2025) that evaluate alignment with user conditions and output quality have been incorporated into the generation process. Recently, test-time alignment methods have shown superior performance compared to parameter-scaling Podell et al. (2024) ; Labs (2024) or fine-tuning approaches Black et al. (2024) ; Wallace et al. (2024) , attracting increasing research interest in this direction Snell et al. (2024) ; Singhal et al. (2025) ; Kim et al. (2026) . Best-of-N (BoN) sampling and Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) Singhal et al. (2025) ; Li et al. (2025) ; Skreta et al. (2025) are widely used test-time alignment methods for diffusion models. However, both approaches have inherent limitations: BoN selects only a single sample, while SMC is prone to particle collapse. As a result, they are primarily suited to scenarios where only one sample is ultimately served. In contrast, guidance-based methods enable the generation of diverse samples by independently adjusting the denoising direction for each sample, making them applicable to settings that require multiple outputs. However, early approaches, such as gradient guidance Kim et al. (2023) ; Bansal et al. (2024) ; Na et al. (2025) , require neural backward passes with differentiable rewards, leading to substantial computational overhead and are prone to reward hacking. Sample-based guidance is emerging as a promising direction, as it can generate diverse samples without requiring neural backward passes. However, it often becomes a computational bottleneck, since iterative rollout sampling requires generating final samples at each time step. Consequently, this line of research has focused on reducing the cost of rollout Potaptchik et al. (2026a) ; Holderrieth et al. (2026) ; Potaptchik et al. (2026b) ; Kim et al. (2026) , and has recently achieved promising results in both performance and efficiency Kim et al. (2026) . However, it still incurs rollout cost, resulting in 2–3× higher sampling cost compared to vanilla sampling. We propose Best-of- N N Guidance (BoNG), a rollout-free, sample-based guidance method inspired by BoN sampling. Unlike Vanilla BoN which uses the reward only once to select the best sample after generation, BoNG performs this selection online and injects it into the reverse diffusion process as a guidance signal ( Figure 1 ). Specifically, we replace the iterative rollout process by selecting the highest-reward expected denoised sample among multiple particles at several intermediate timesteps. This approach steers all samples toward the direction of the highest-reward sample without incurring additional feed-forward computations of the score network. We theoretically analyze its connection to the reward-tilted distribution targeted by prior work, and empirically demonstrate gains over Vanilla BoN, SMC, and prior guidance methods with minimal additional inference cost. Figure 1: Best-of- N N Guidance (BoNG) (Left) Vanilla BoN sampling selects the highest-reward sample only after generation. (Middle) BoNG performs online BoN selection ( Algorithm 1 ) and uses the selected sample to guide the remaining particles ( Algorithm 2 ). (Right) BoNG consistently improves single-output performance over Vanilla BoN and SMC across various sample budgets.

(2024) ; Domingo-Enrich et al. (2025) . SMC methods Singhal et al. (2025) ; Li et al. (2025) ; Skreta et al. (2025) generate multiple samples from the base diffusion model and perform resampling based on intermediate reward values. However, SMC suffers from particle collapse, which degrades the quality of the best sample in single-output generation and limits sample diversity in multi-output settings. Gradient-guidance methods address this issue by enabling i.i.d. sampling by approximating the target time-dependent score function. However, these methods require either training diffusion time-conditioned reward models Kim et al. (2023) or performing multiple neural backward passes with Taylor approximation Bansal et al. (2024) ; Na et al. (2025) at every denoising step, resulting in significant latency and memory overhead. Sample-based guidance methods Potaptchik et al. (2026a) ; Kim et al. (2026) have recently emerged as a promising direction because they avoid particle collapse and do not require neural backward propagation for guidance. Tilt Potaptchik et al. (2026a) proposes a gradient-free method for incorporating expected future rewards into the reverse process. However, it remains computationally expensive because it requires generating multiple samples from 𝐱 t {\mathbf{x}}_{t} to 𝐱 0 {\mathbf{x}}_{0} at every timestep t t , known as backward rollout. GlassFlow Holderrieth et al. (2026) improves efficiency by reducing the number of rollout steps through ODE-based sampling, and MFM Potaptchik et al. (2026b) further accelerates this process by replacing the ODE solver with a distilled model. LiDAR Kim et al. (2026) proposes a forward rollout strategy for estimating intermediate rewards. This reduces per-step rollout sampling to a single marginal rollout. LiDAR significantly improves sample-based guidance and achieves state-of-the-art performance while being around 10× faster than gradient-guidance methods. However, it still requires additional lookahead sampling, making it 2–3× slower than vanilla diffusion sampling. The goal of this work is to develop an efficient and effective sample-based guidance method inspired by the idea of BoN sampling.

sections.heading: 3.2 Test-time Human Alignment
sections.text: Problem Setup: With the advancement of diffusion models, many pre-trained models are now available as open-source Rombach et al. (2022) ; Podell et al. (2024) ; Labs (2024) , enabling generation conditioned on user input 𝐜 {\mathbf{c}} . However, the final generated sample 𝐱 0 {\mathbf{x}}_{0} often does not align well with the user input 𝐜 {\mathbf{c}} . Accordingly, we assume access to a pre-trained diffusion model p θ ​ ( 𝐱 0 | 𝐜 ) p_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{0}|{\mathbf{c}}) and a human preference reward function r : 𝒳 0 × 𝒞 → ℝ r:\mathcal{X}_{0}\times\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} , and aim to obtain samples 𝐱 0 {\mathbf{x}}_{0} such that reward r ⁡ ( 𝐱 0 , 𝐜 ) r({\mathbf{x}}_{0},{\mathbf{c}}) is high, by manipulating the inference process. Here, 𝒳 0 \mathcal{X}_{0} denotes the data space at time t = 0 t=0 , and 𝒞 \mathcal{C} denotes the user’s input condition space.

sections.heading: 3.2.1 Best-of- N N Sampling
sections.text: Best-of- N N (BoN) sampling is a post-hoc selection procedure that draws N N i.i.d. samples from the base distribution p θ ​ ( 𝐱 0 ∣ 𝐜 ) p_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{0}\mid{\mathbf{c}}) and returns a single sample with the highest reward. In finite N N , the BoN sample from the base distribution is defined as: 𝐱 0 BoN := argmax { 𝐱 0 i } i = 1 N ​ r ​ ( 𝐱 0 i , 𝐜 ) , 𝐱 0 i ​ ∼ i.i.d. ​ p θ ​ ( 𝐱 0 ∣ 𝐜 ) \displaystyle{{\mathbf{x}}}_{0}^{\mathrm{BoN}}:=\underset{\{{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}}{\operatorname{argmax}}\;\;r({{\mathbf{x}}}_{0}^{i},{\mathbf{c}}),\qquad{{\mathbf{x}}}_{0}^{i}\overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim}p_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{0}\mid{\mathbf{c}}) (2) BoN sampling is a remarkably strong inference-time alignment strategy in practice Ichihara et al. (2025) , since it can substantially improve the quality of the final selected sample by increasing N N , without modifying the underlying generative model. However, it remains fundamentally inefficient: the sampling process is done by Eq. 1 , reward information is not used during the generation process. As a result, obtaining a sample from a high-reward region may require large N N . Moreover, BoN sampling is inherently designed to return a single best output, and therefore does not directly address the multi-output setting Microsoft Team (2026) ; xAI Team (2026) in which all N N generated candidates are expected to be of high quality.

sections.heading: 4.3 Instantiation of BoNG
sections.text: BoNG can be applied flexibly during inference time, which allows the method to interpolate between aggressive reward optimization and diversity preservation. Similarly to SMC Singhal et al. (2025) , we instantiate BoNG by specifying a guidance timestep window, i.e. the subset of reverse diffusion steps at which the BoN guidance term is activated. The guidance window determines how often the particle population is steered toward the current Best-of- N N target during reverse diffusion. Applying BoNG over more timesteps yields stronger steering toward high-reward regions, whereas restricting the window leaves more denoising steps governed by the original diffusion process. In this sense, the guidance timestep window in BoNG plays a role analogous to the reward-strength hyperparameter λ \lambda in prior methods Bansal et al. (2024) ; Na et al. (2025) ; Li et al. (2025) targeting the reward-tilted distribution in Eq. 3 . Consistent with Theorem 4.3 , increasing the guidance window corresponds to a more reward-tilted target distribution. In addition, following prior guidance methods Chung et al. (2024) ; Ho and Salimans (2021) , we introduce a guidance scale multiplying the BoN guidance term in Eq. 7 . This provides an additional degree of control over the magnitude of guidance at each timestep. Further analysis of BoNG is provided in Appendices C and D.1 .

sections.heading: 5.1 Single-Output Performance
sections.text: As shown in Table 1 , BoNG consistently outperforms baselines across different backbone models with varying sample budget N N . Over 36 comparisons, BoNG achieves the highest score in 29 cases, ranking first in 80.56% of all comparisons against baselines. Even with 2 particles, BoNG shows steep performance gains over baselines and further shows superior performance across N = 2 , 3 , 4 N=2,3,4 . In particular, BoNG with N = 4 N=4 outperforms Vanilla BoN with N = 8 N=8 in GenEval (see Figure 1 ). This advantage scales to larger budgets where BoNG continues to outperform SMC and Vanilla BoN (see Section 5.2 ). Overall, these results demonstrate that even with small N N budget, BoNG outputs a high reward sample compared to Vanilla BoN and SMC. BoNG is also applicable to modern flow-matching backbones, retaining its advantage on FLUX.1-dev (12B) Labs (2024) ( Section 5.2 ).

sections.heading: Why does BoNG outperform SMC?
sections.text: SMC also steers the generative process by incorporating reward information by interaction of particles, similar to BoNG. The main difference is that SMC relies on resampling, whereas BoNG does not. In SMC, even if denoising starts from N N independent particles, repeated resampling based on intermediate rewards can collapse the particle population onto only a few trajectories, or even a single one. Such particle collapse reduces exploration and degrades the quality of the final Best-of- N N sample. In contrast, BoNG preserves all particles and instead performs Best-of- N N selection in the predicted clean-sample space at each intermediate timestep. The selected high-reward target is then used as a guidance signal so that the particle population is steered to high-reward regions without particle copy. As a result, BoNG maintains a better exploration-exploitation tradeoff than SMC, which leads to stronger final BoN performance under the same particle budget. Moreover, since guidance and resampling act on different components of the particle system, the two are composable: applying BoNG on top of SMC improves both the mean and the BoN reward at every particle count ( Section F.4 ).

sections.heading: 5.2 Multi-Output Performance
sections.text: As shown in Table 2 , BoNG achieves the best performance across all three metrics, demonstrating that its benefit is not limited to improving only the final selected sample (BoN) but also for overall samples. More importantly, these gains are obtained with very small test-time overhead. Compared with prior guidance methods, BoNG shows the strongest average performance while remaining close to vanilla diffusion sampling in inference time.

sections.heading: Why does BoNG outperform prior guidance methods?
sections.text: These results are consistent with Theorem 4.3 , which shows that BoNG can also be interpreted as a sample-based guidance method targeting the reward-tilted distribution Eq. 3 . Its strong empirical performance comes from combining this connection with the core strength of Best-of- N N sampling: selecting a single high-reward output from N N generated candidates. Rather than applying Best-of- N N sampling only after generation, BoNG injects the same principle directly into reverse diffusion by repeatedly using the current Best-of- N N target to steer the denoising particle population toward higher-reward regions. At the same time, unlike prior sample-based guidance methods, BoNG does not require additional forward or backward rollouts to construct guidance samples. Instead, it directly reuses the base scores and one-step denoised samples of particles already present in the denoising process. As a result, BoNG inherits the strong best-sample behavior of Best-of- N N sampling while avoiding the computational overhead of prior guidance methods, leading to a substantially better efficiency performance tradeoff of the overall quality of multiple generated samples. sections.heading: Reward-Diversity Trade-off against SMC.
sections.text: Similar to BoNG, SMC can also be adapted to the multi-output setting. SMC does it by tuning the reward-weighting parameter λ \lambda that determines particle potentials, whereas BoNG controls the guidance time window in Section 4.3 . Section 5.2 shows that BoNG achieves a consistently better reward-diversity Pareto frontier than SMC. SMC incorporates reward information through resampling, which necessarily duplicates some particles and removes others, while BoNG incorporates reward information through guidance and thus modifies particle trajectories more gradually. Consequently, BoNG preserves diversity more effectively while maintaining strong reward improvement, giving it a clear advantage in the multi-output setting.

sections.heading: Efficiency–Performance comparison among gradient guidance methods.
sections.text: The guidance baselines in Table 2 incur substantial additional computation: UG and DATE require backward passes through the score and reward models, and LiDAR requires additional lookahead rollouts with score-network evaluations (see Section D.2 for the full cost breakdown). BoNG avoids both sources of overhead, yet achieves better average performance than LiDAR. We attribute this to the construction of the guidance signal: LiDAR relies on random lookahead samples, whereas BoNG steers all particles toward the current highest-reward denoising particle. Table 2 extends the efficiency–performance Pareto points of Table 2 , showing how performance changes as more computation is used; BoNG achieves the steepest performance gain relative to the amount of computation.

sections.heading: Performance with different reward functions.
sections.text: Section 5.2 shows results when BoNG is guided by CLIP, ImageReward (IR), or their weighted combination. To account for the different reward scales, we Z-score normalize each reward before applying the mixing weights. As the CLIP weight increases, the generated samples achieve higher CLIP scores, whereas increasing the IR weight improves ImageReward scores. This trend shows that BoNG can effectively leverage other reward functions as guidance signals. Furthermore, combining IR and CLIP yields a clear trade-off curve between the two metrics. The mixed rewards produce frontier points, indicating that reward mixing can improve the balance across complementary evaluation metrics. These results suggest that BoNG provides a reward-agnostic guidance mechanism that can operate with different reward functions and can further benefit from combining multiple rewards. We further test HPSv2 ( Wu et al., 2023 ) as the guidance reward in Section 5.2 , where BoNG improves both the mean and the BoN scores over Vanilla, confirming that the guidance mechanism transfers to a different human-preference reward. Results with a heavier reward model are provided in Section F.3 .

sections.heading: Budget-matched comparison with LiDAR.
sections.text: Table 1 compares methods whose end-to-end cost stays close to that of Vanilla BoN sampling. LiDAR ( Kim et al., 2026 ) , a representative sample-based guidance method, can also serve the single-output setting, but its cost is higher: independently of N N , it must first generate n n lookahead samples in advance, each requiring δ \delta score-network evaluations, and its performance is governed by n n (see Section D.2 for the full cost breakdown). We therefore compare BoNG against LiDAR under matched end-to-end wall-clock time, trading off N N against n n for LiDAR. As shown in Section 5.2 , BoNG achieves the best results on every metric with the shortest generation time. This is because BoNG constructs its guidance signal from the N N particles currently being sampled, whereas LiDAR relies on separately generated lookahead samples. Additional experiments are provided in Section F.2 .

sections.heading: Scalability of BoNG.
sections.text: BoNG scales with both the sample budget and the backbone. Section 5.2 shows that on SD v1.5 (DDPM 100 steps), BoNG consistently outperforms SMC and Vanilla BoN for N ∈ { 8 , 16 , 32 } N\in\{8,16,32\} , and its BoN performance keeps improving with N N , inheriting the scaling behavior of Best-of- N N sampling. BoNG also benefits from a stronger generative process: in Table 1 , its performance increases as the backbone grows from SD v1.5 (0.9B) to SDXL (2.6B) and as the sampler becomes more accurate (DDIM 50 to DDPM 100 steps). This trend extends to flow-matching backbones, to which BoNG applies directly since it requires only the one-step denoised estimate in Eq. 5 . On FLUX.1-dev (12B) ( Labs, 2024 ) , Section 5.2 shows that BoNG continues to improve over Vanilla BoN at every N N , confirming that its gains carry over to a larger and stronger backbone.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We propose BoNG, a test-time alignment method that integrates Best-of- N N sampling directly into the reverse diffusion process of diffusion models. By performing online Best-of- N N selection among denoising particles, BoNG steers particles to high reward regions during generation rather than using rewards only for post-hoc selection. We further show that BoNG is theoretically connected to sample-based guidance for reward-tilted diffusion sampling, while avoiding the costly rollout procedure required by prior methods. Empirically, BoNG improves both single-output (BoN) performance and average multi-output quality, achieving strong alignment gains with minimal additional inference cost. These results demonstrate that BoNG is an efficient and flexible framework for test-time diffusion alignment.

sections.heading: Limitations and Future Work.
sections.text: BoNG assumes that the reward model faithfully reflects the target preference; an inaccurate reward model can steer the particles toward unwanted regions, a limitation shared by all reward-based alignment methods. As future work, the finite- λ \lambda relaxation in Appendix E , which replaces the hard Best-of- N N selection with a soft-weighted posterior mean, opens a promising direction: exploring this relaxation in greater depth, for example by scaling λ \lambda to control the strength of alignment, would be a meaningful extension of BoNG.

sections.heading: B.1 Experiment Setup
sections.text: We use SD v1.5 [ 22 ] and SDXL [ 19 ] backbones with CFG [ 9 ] scale 7.5 for all experiments. For each backbone, we experiment with the DDPM 100-step sampler and the DDIM 50-step sampler (probability-flow ODE) in Table 1 , the latter being substantially faster. We additionally evaluate on the flow-matching backbone FLUX.1-dev [ 14 ] , using the flow-matching Euler sampler with 28 steps and guidance scale 3.5. All results are averaged over three random seeds, except FLUX.1-dev, which uses a single seed due to computational cost.

sections.heading: B.2 BoNG Configuration
sections.text: BoNG has three hyperparameters: the window position t start t_{\mathrm{start}} , the window size K K , and the guidance scale s s . The selection protocol and the corresponding sensitivity analyses are given in Appendices C and D ; here we record the values used in the main experiments. For a compute budget comparable to the SMC baseline [ 24 ] , which performs five resampling steps, we set the number of guided transitions to K ≤ 4 K\leq 4 in all configurations of Table 1 . A guidance window [ t start , t end ] [t_{\mathrm{start}},t_{\mathrm{end}}] denotes the set of guided transitions t → t + 1 t\to t+1 for t start ≤ t < t end t_{\mathrm{start}}\leq t<t_{\mathrm{end}} ; e.g., [ 40 , 44 ] [40,44] denotes the four transitions 40 → 41 , … , 43 → 44 40\to 41,\dots,43\to 44 ( K = 4 K=4 ). The guidance windows are [ 40 , 44 ] [40,44] for SD v1.5 with DDPM 100 steps (where step 40 corresponds to t = 0.6 t=0.6 , with t = 1 t=1 the prior and t = 0 t=0 the data), [ 21 , 23 ] [21,23] for SD v1.5 with DDIM 50 steps, [ 24 , 28 ] [24,28] for SDXL with DDPM 100 steps, [ 20 , 22 ] [20,22] for SDXL with DDIM 50 steps, [ 12 , 14 ] [12,14] for FLUX with Euler 28 steps. The guidance scale is s = 6 s=6 for SD v1.5, s = 4 s=4 for SDXL, s = 2 s=2 for FLUX. Table 2 uses the same configuration as Table 1 .

sections.heading: B.3 Baseline Configuration
sections.text: We apply the shared settings of Section B.1 to all baselines. In Table 1 , Vanilla runs standard diffusion sampling N N times and selects the best sample according to ImageReward [ 36 ] . The baseline denoted SMC is FK-Steering [ 24 ] under its recommended text-to-image configuration: max potential, λ = 10 \lambda=10 , five evenly spaced resampling steps, adaptive resampling, and intermediate rewards on denoised estimates. Best- k k -of- N N involves no guidance: N = 5 N=5 samples are generated with the base model, and the top k = 4 k=4 samples by reward are returned. For Table 2 , we follow the standard practice of quoting the reported numbers for LiDAR [ 13 ] , UG [ 2 ] , and DATE [ 18 ] from the concurrent work LiDAR, which achieves state-of-the-art performance in the multi-output setting. Please refer to Sections B.1 and B.2 of LiDAR for the corresponding configurations. For transparency, we additionally reproduce all baselines of Table 2 in our unified codebase under the same configurations and report the results in Section F.1 .

sections.heading: B.4 Evaluation Metrics
sections.text: We report the metrics used throughout our experiments. ImageReward [ 36 ] : a learned human-preference reward model for text-to-image generation. It assigns a scalar preference score to each generated image conditioned on the text prompt, and we use it to evaluate overall image quality and prompt satisfaction from a human-centric perspective. CLIP Score [ 7 ] : measures the semantic alignment between the text prompt and the generated image by computing the similarity between their CLIP embeddings. It provides a reference-free estimate of prompt-image correspondence, although it may be less sensitive to fine-grained compositional errors. GenEval [ 6 ] : an object-centric evaluation benchmark for text-to-image generation. It uses detection-based checks to assess whether generated images correctly satisfy prompt-specified entities, attributes, counts, and spatial relations, making it useful for measuring compositional accuracy. We measure the diversity of generated samples by computing pairwise distances in the CLIP image-embedding space, following the evaluation protocol of FK-Steering. 1 1 1 https://github.com/zacharyhorvitz/D-Diffusion-Steering/blob/main/text_to_image/fkd_diffusers/rewards.py

sections.heading: Appendix C Hyperparameter Selection Protocol of BoNG
sections.text: BoNG has three hyperparameters: the window position t start t_{\mathrm{start}} , the window size K K , and the guidance scale s s . For a new backbone or sampler, we set them by the following protocol: • Window position t start t_{\mathrm{start}} : place the window where the correlation between the Tweedie-estimate reward r ⁡ ( 𝐱 ^ 0 ) r(\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}_{0}) and the final reward becomes reliable ( ≈ 0.6 \approx 0.6 ). • Window size K K : choose K K by the compute budget, at or below the resampling budget of the SMC baseline. • Guidance scale s s : tune s ∈ [ 1 , 6 ] s\in[1,6] to select the desired point on the reward–diversity frontier, at no extra compute. This procedure was followed for every configuration in the paper. The remainder of this section justifies each rule with controlled experiments: Section C.1 shows why the window position trades off the accuracy of the guidance signal against the steerability of the samples, Section C.2 shows that the window size moves gradually and monotonically along the reward–diversity frontier, and Section C.3 shows that the guidance scale sweeps the same frontier at zero additional cost.

sections.heading: C.1 Window Position
sections.text: A meaningful guidance signal requires the one-step denoised estimate 𝐱 ^ 0 BoN \hat{{\mathbf{x}}}_{0}^{\mathrm{BoN}} to be aligned with the final reward, so we place the window near the point where the correlation between r ⁡ ( 𝐱 ^ 0 ) r(\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}_{0}) and the final reward exceeds 0.6 0.6 (cf. Figure 5 of FK-Steering [ 24 ] ). Placing the window too late is ineffective for the opposite reason: by then the high-level features of each sample are already determined, so particles committed to low-reward regions can no longer be steered. An early window ( [ 20 , 24 ] [20,24] ) fails on both metrics because the Tweedie-reward correlation is still low. sections.heading: D.1 Effect of Guidance Timestep Window
sections.text: The guidance timestep window jointly determines reward optimization, diversity preservation, and inference-time overhead. As discussed in Sections 4.3 and 5.3 , the window plays the role of λ \lambda in the reward-tilted distribution: applying BoNG over more timesteps yields stronger reward optimization, but may reduce sample diversity by making the generation process closer to sampling from a highly reward-tilted distribution. At the same time, the window size sets the additional cost N ​ K ​ ( D + R ) NK(D+R) of BoNG ( Section D.2 ). Section 5.2 shows the resulting reward–diversity trade-off, Table 7 confirms that both effects are gradual and monotone, and Table 2 shows that BoNG achieves the best performance–efficiency trade-off among the compared methods; the selection rules for the window are given in Appendix C .

sections.heading: D.2 Computational Cost
sections.text: BoNG introduces no extra score network evaluations over Vanilla diffusion sampling. sections.heading: Appendix E Finite- λ \lambda Soft Relaxation of BoNG
sections.text: BoNG applies hard Best-of- N N selection over the one-step denoised candidates and therefore corresponds to the large- λ \lambda limit described in Theorem 4.3 . However, Lemma 4.2 itself holds for every finite λ > 0 \lambda>0 , and the same rollout-free one-step Tweedie construction admits a natural finite- λ \lambda relaxation, which we derive and evaluate in this section. We emphasize that this relaxation is a variant beyond the hard-selection algorithm evaluated in the main experiments; all results in the main text correspond to the hard-selection BoNG.

sections.text: This construction remains approximate in two respects. First, the one-step Tweedie estimates are deterministic posterior means rather than exact proposal samples from p θ ​ ( 𝐱 0 ∣ 𝐜 ) p_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{0}\mid{\mathbf{c}}) . Consequently, the exact importance-sampling interpretation of Lemma 4.2 does not directly transfer to this rollout-free relaxation: BoNG admits a rollout-free finite- λ \lambda relaxation, rather than exactly targeting the finite- λ \lambda reward-tilted distribution.

sections.heading: F.4 Composing BoNG with SMC
sections.text: Inference-time steering methods fall into two distinct classes [ 24 ] : reward-guidance methods, which steer particles by modifying the sampling dynamics, and particle-based resampling methods, which steer by reweighting and resampling intermediate particles with potentials. BoNG shares a structural connection with SMC, as both maintain N N interacting particles and evaluate intermediate rewards on denoised estimates, but the two belong to different classes. BoNG is a reward-guidance method, in which the reward signal enters through the guidance term s σ t 2 ​ ( 𝐱 ^ 0 BoN − 𝐱 ^ 0 i ) \frac{s}{\sigma_{t}^{2}}\bigl(\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}_{0}^{\mathrm{BoN}}-\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}_{0}^{i}\bigr) added to the score function, whereas SMC is a potential-based resampling method, in which the reward signal enters through the resampling weights G t G_{t} while the transition kernel is left unchanged. Concretely, while the outer loop of BoNG resembles that of SMC (propagate N N particles, score their denoised estimates with the reward), SMC applies multinomial resampling based on G t G_{t} , so particles are copied and deleted, whereas BoNG applies no resampling and instead modifies the score function. In this sense, BoNG brings the strength of the guidance class, with no particle copying or deletion, to the black-box reward setting. This distinction has a direct practical consequence: since guidance and resampling act on different components of the particle system (the transition kernel and the resampling weights, respectively), they are orthogonal and composable. To verify this empirically, we apply BoNG on top of SMC and report ImageReward with N N particles in Table 16 , for both the mean over the N N returned samples and the Best-of- N N sample. Composing BoNG with SMC improves both the mean and the Best-of- N N reward at every particle count, with no reward gradients and no additional score-network evaluations. This empirically confirms that BoNG occupies the proposal-generator slot of the FK-IPS framework [ 24 ] and complements resampling-based steering. Table 16: Composing BoNG with SMC. A simple yet effective algorithm for test-time alignment is Best-of- N N (BoN) sampling, which draws N N i.i.d. samples from a pre-trained diffusion model and outputs the single highest-reward sample. Despite its empirical success, BoN makes limited use of reward information, as it is incorporated only at the final selection stage without influencing the reverse diffusion trajectory during sampling. Consequently, BoN sampling does not improve the average alignment of generated samples and is primarily suited to single-output settings. We propose Best-of- N N Guidance (BoNG), a novel method that integrates the principle of BoN sampling directly into the reverse diffusion process. BoNG performs online BoN selection over denoising particles and adjusts the reverse diffusion process to steer the particle population toward higher-reward regions during generation. Specifically, by introducing an asymmetric guidance interaction among denoising particles, BoNG uses the current BoN particle as a guidance signal to the rest of the particle population. This particle-level interaction reshapes the sampling process toward higher-reward regions, enabling BoNG to improve not only the final best sample beyond Vanilla BoN sampling, but also the average quality of generated samples. Over 36 empirical comparisons, BoNG achieves the best performance in 29 cases, ranking first in 80.56% of the comparisons against SMC and Vanilla BoN sampling. BoNG also supports multi-output capability, achieving 1.3 × 	imes ImageReward score of the latest sample-based guidance method with a 1.6 × 	imes speedup. We release the code at https://github.com/aailab-kaist/BoNG . 1 Introduction Diffusion models Sohl-Dickstein et al. (2015) ; Ho et al. (2020) ; Song et al. (2021) demonstrate strong generative capabilities, leading to a growing number of real-world applications that produce outputs conditioned on user inputs Microsoft Team (2026) ; xAI Team (2026) . However, the generated outputs still do not fully align with user preferences in terms of input alignment and sample fidelity. To address this issue, reward functions Xu et al. (2023) ; Wu et al. (2023) ; Ma et al. (2025) that evaluate alignment with user conditions and output quality have been incorporated into the generation process. Recently, test-time alignment methods have shown superior performance compared to parameter-scaling Podell et al. (2024) ; Labs (2024) or fine-tuning approaches Black et al. (2024) ; Wallace et al. (2024) , attracting increasing research interest in this direction Snell et al. (2024) ; Singhal et al. (2025) ; Kim et al. (2026) . Best-of-N (BoN) sampling and Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) Singhal et al. (2025) ; Li et al. (2025) ; Skreta et al. (2025) are widely used test-time alignment methods for diffusion models. However, both approaches have inherent limitations: BoN selects only a single sample, while SMC is prone to particle collapse. As a result, they are primarily suited to scenarios where only one sample is ultimately served. In contrast, guidance-based methods enable the generation of diverse samples by independently adjusting the denoising direction for each sample, making them applicable to settings that require multiple outputs. However, early approaches, such as gradient guidance Kim et al. (2023) ; Bansal et al. (2024) ; Na et al. (2025) , require neural backward passes with differentiable rewards, leading to substantial computational overhead and are prone to reward hacking. Sample-based guidance is emerging as a promising direction, as it can generate diverse samples without requiring neural backward passes. However, it often becomes a computational bottleneck, since iterative rollout sampling requires generating final samples at each time step. Consequently, this line of research has focused on reducing the cost of rollout Potaptchik et al. (2026a) ; Holderrieth et al. (2026) ; Potaptchik et al. (2026b) ; Kim et al. (2026) , and has recently achieved promising results in both performance and efficiency Kim et al. (2026) . However, it still incurs rollout cost, resulting in 2–3× higher sampling cost compared to vanilla sampling. We propose Best-of- N N Guidance (BoNG), a rollout-free, sample-based guidance method inspired by BoN sampling. Unlike Vanilla BoN which uses the reward only once to select the best sample after generation, BoNG performs this selection online and injects it into the reverse diffusion process as a guidance signal ( Figure 1 ). Specifically, we replace the iterative rollout process by selecting the highest-reward expected denoised sample among multiple particles at several intermediate timesteps. This approach steers all samples toward the direction of the highest-reward sample without incurring additional feed-forward computations of the score network. We theoretically analyze its connection to the reward-tilted distribution targeted by prior work, and empirically demonstrate gains over Vanilla BoN, SMC, and prior guidance methods with minimal additional inference cost. Over 36 comparisons, BoNG achieves the highest score in 29 cases, ranking first in 80.56% of all comparisons against baselines. Even with 2 particles, BoNG shows steep performance gains over baselines and further shows superior performance across N = 2 , 3 , 4 N=2,3,4 . In particular, BoNG with N = 4 N=4 outperforms Vanilla BoN with N = 8 N=8 in GenEval (see Figure 1 ). This advantage scales to larger budgets where BoNG continues to outperform SMC and Vanilla BoN (see Section 5.2 ). Overall, these results demonstrate that even with small N N budget, BoNG outputs a high reward sample compared to Vanilla BoN and SMC. BoNG is also applicable to modern flow-matching backbones, retaining its advantage on FLUX.1-dev (12B) Labs (2024) ( Section 5.2 ). Why does BoNG outperform SMC? SMC also steers the generative process by incorporating reward information by interaction of particles, similar to BoNG. The main difference is that SMC relies on resampling, whereas BoNG does not. In SMC, even if denoising starts from N N independent particles, repeated resampling based on intermediate rewards can collapse the particle population onto only a few trajectories, or even a single one. Such particle collapse reduces exploration and degrades the quality of the final Best-of- N N sample. In contrast, BoNG preserves all particles and instead performs Best-of- N N selection in the predicted clean-sample space at each intermediate timestep. The selected high-reward target is then used as a guidance signal so that the particle population is steered to high-reward regions without particle copy. As a result, BoNG maintains a better exploration-exploitation tradeoff than SMC, which leads to stronger final BoN performance under the same particle budget. Moreover, since guidance and resampling act on different components of the particle system, the two are composable: applying BoNG on top of SMC improves both the mean and the BoN reward at every particle count ( Section F.4 ). 5.2 Multi-Output Performance As shown in Table 2 , BoNG achieves the best performance across all three metrics, demonstrating that its benefit is not limited to improving only the final selected sample (BoN) but also for overall samples. More importantly, these gains are obtained with very small test-time overhead. Compared with prior guidance methods, BoNG shows the strongest average performance while remaining close to vanilla diffusion sampling in inference time. Why does BoNG outperform prior guidance methods? These results are consistent with Theorem 4.3 , which shows that BoNG can also be interpreted as a sample-based guidance method targeting the reward-tilted distribution Eq. 3 . Its strong empirical performance comes from combining this connection with the core strength of Best-of- N N sampling: selecting a single high-reward output from N N generated candidates. Rather than applying Best-of- N N sampling only after generation, BoNG injects the same principle directly into reverse diffusion by repeatedly using the current Best-of- N N target to steer the denoising particle population toward higher-reward regions. At the same time, unlike prior sample-based guidance methods, BoNG does not require additional forward or backward rollouts to construct guidance samples. Instead, it directly reuses the base scores and one-step denoised samples of particles already present in the denoising process.
